# Google and the Attention Monopoly {#sec-4-12}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1998–2004
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does advertising become a surveillance infrastructure?

**The answer.** By selling intent instead of space. Page and Brin's own doctoral
paper argued that advertising-funded search engines would be structurally biased
against their users — and then they built the largest advertising-funded search
engine in history. The AdWords auction turned the moment a person states a
desire into a priced, contested asset.

**The mechanism.** Chokepoint control of an input nobody had previously
identified: human intention. The chapter's power comes from the founders' own
documented warning, which is a primary source that indicts the outcome more
effectively than any critic could.

**The key fact.** The original PageRank-era paper contains an explicit appendix
arguing that advertising creates incentives to degrade search quality and that a
transparent, academically oriented engine is therefore necessary. It is the
clearest self-indictment in the history of technology, and it is a citable
primary document.

**The human anchor.** Two graduate students writing a warning about the business
model they are about to adopt, and then adopting it. The chapter should be
genuinely sympathetic — the paper is honest, the pressures were real, and that
is why it matters.

**Excluded voices.** Everyone whose behavioural data constitutes the asset
without compensation or meaningful consent, and the publishers whose content
became the index's raw material. Also the advertisers on the other side of an
auction whose rules they cannot inspect.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the attention chokepoint was understood in
advance by the people who built it by quoting their own published warning
against it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Larry Page and Sergey Brin's original paper on their search engine contains an
appendix arguing that advertising-funded search engines are structurally biased
against their users, that the incentives push toward degrading results, and that
a transparent, academically oriented engine is therefore necessary. They then
built the largest advertising-funded search engine in history. It is the
clearest self-indictment in the history of technology, and it is a citable
primary document.

The chapter is genuinely sympathetic, which is what makes it work. The technical
insight was real: link structure was a far better relevance signal than keyword
matching, and PageRank produced results that were obviously superior. Stanford
held the patent, licensed it to the company, and took shares — Bayh-Dole from
the previous chapter, with a number attached. The funding came from Kleiner
Perkins and Sequoia, both of them, which returns the story to Sand Hill Road.

And the revenue problem was real too. They tried licensing search to portals and
it did not generate enough. The chapter walks through what was attempted before
advertising, because that is what makes the turn credible rather than cynical.

AdWords, refined between 2000 and 2002 into an auction with quality scoring and
cost-per-click pricing, was elegant and enormously effective. Its significance
is what it made tradeable. A search query is a stated desire, timestamped and
addressable, which is worth far more than a magazine page — and the chapter's
argument is that the chokepoint here is human intention itself, a resource
nobody had previously identified as ownable.

Then the appendix is set against the outcome, without editorial comment. The
juxtaposition is the argument.

The excluded are the users whose behavioural data constitutes the asset without
compensation or meaningful consent, the publishers whose content became index
material, and the advertisers bidding inside an auction whose rules they cannot
inspect.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** Quote the appendix. Their words, before the company existed.
2. **The technical insight.** PageRank and why link structure was a better
   relevance signal. Enough to see the advantage.
3. **Stanford's stake.** The patent, licensed from the university, and the
   shares Stanford held. Bayh-Dole from ch. 10 in action, with a number
   attached.
4. **1998-1999.** Incorporation, the Menlo Park garage, and the funding —
   including both Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia, which returns to ch. 5's
   corridor.
5. **The revenue problem.** What they tried before advertising. This beat earns
   the reader's sympathy and makes the turn credible.
6. **AdWords, 2000-2002.** The auction, quality score, and the shift to cost-
   per-click. Explain the mechanism properly; its elegance is part of the
   argument.
7. **Intent as the asset.** Why a search query is worth more than a magazine
   page: it is a stated desire, timestamped and addressable.
8. **Return to the appendix.** Set the warning against the outcome. No
   editorialising; the juxtaposition is the argument.
9. **The excluded.** Users as uncompensated data sources; publishers as raw
   material; advertisers inside an opaque auction.
10. **Landing.** The chokepoint is no longer physical, legal, or even
   informational. It is attentional, and it is the most profitable one anyone
   has found.

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does advertising become a surveillance infrastructure?
:::

The paper that described Google contains an appendix explaining why Google
should not exist.

Sergey Brin and Larry Page, then doctoral students at Stanford, published "The
Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine" in 1998. Its final
appendix argues that advertising-funded search engines are inherently biased
toward the advertisers and away from the needs of consumers, that the bias is
insidious because it is difficult for users to detect, and that these incentives
mean a search engine of this kind will be crafted to serve the advertiser rather
than the searcher.

They concluded that it is crucial to have a competitive search engine that is
transparent and in the academic realm.

Then they built the largest advertising-funded search engine in history, and by
any measure the most profitable business ever constructed on the mechanism they
had just described.

## The insight

The technical contribution was real and it deserves a fair account, because the
chapter is stronger if the reader understands why the thing worked.

Search engines in 1997 ranked pages primarily by the text on them, which meant
anyone could rank highly by repeating a word. PageRank used a different signal:
the structure of links between pages. A page linked to by many pages is probably
useful, and a link from a page that is itself heavily linked counts for more
than one from a page nobody reads. It is a recursive measure of authority, and
it was much harder to fake because it depended on the behaviour of other people.

The results were obviously better, and anyone who used the web in 1998 remembers
the difference.

## Stanford's position

The university owned the patent.

PageRank was developed on federally funded research at Stanford — the Digital
Libraries project, supported by the National Science Foundation among others —
and under the Bayh-Dole arrangement described two chapters ago the university
took title. It licensed the patent to the company, exclusively, in exchange for
a fee and shares.

Stanford sold most of those shares a few years after the 2004 public offering,
for a sum in the region of three hundred million dollars.

That transaction is the entire book in a single line item. Federal research
funding produces an invention; a statute assigns the invention to the
university; the university licenses it to a company founded by its own doctoral
students; the company becomes one of the most valuable enterprises on earth; and
the university collects a nine-figure return.

Public money in, private monopoly out, institution enriched, elite reproduced.
There is no step in that sequence that is hidden, illegal, or even unusual.

## The revenue problem

The chapter has to give the turn honestly, because a cynical account of it would
be wrong.

Google's initial business plan was to license its search technology to portals,
and it did — to Yahoo, among others. The revenue was insufficient to support the
infrastructure the index required, and the infrastructure requirement grew with
the web. They tried other approaches. The venture funding, which came from both
Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia in an unusual arrangement in 1999, brought
expectations of a real business model.

Advertising was what worked, and it worked so well that within a few years no
alternative was conceivable.

## AdWords

The mechanism was elegant and the chapter should explain it properly, because
its elegance is part of the argument.

Advertisers bid on search terms. But the auction did not simply sell the top
position to the highest bidder. Google introduced a quality score — a measure of
how likely users were to click a given advertisement — and ranked ads by the
combination of bid and quality. An advertiser with a more relevant advertisement
could outrank one paying more.

Advertisers paid per click rather than per impression, which meant they paid
only when the system had actually delivered someone. And the auction was
structured so that bidding one's true valuation was approximately the right
strategy.

The result aligned three interests that ordinarily conflict. Users got
advertisements that were more relevant. Advertisers paid for outcomes rather
than exposure. And Google captured a share of the value of every commercial
intention expressed anywhere in its index.

## Intent as an asset

Here is what the auction actually monetised, and it had not previously been
identified as a thing that could be owned.

A magazine advertisement reaches people who happen to be reading a magazine. A
television advertisement reaches people who happen to be watching. Both are sold
on demographics, which is a guess about who is present.

A search query is different in kind. It is a person stating, in their own words,
at a specific moment, what they are trying to find. It is a declared intention,
timestamped and immediately actionable, and its commercial value is
correspondingly enormous.

Google did not invent human intention and did not create the demand. It occupied
the position between a stated desire and the market that could satisfy it, and
priced the passage — which is what the Southern Pacific did to freight in Act
II, what the studios did to films in chapter 8, and what Microsoft did to
applications in chapter 9.

Each of these is the same chokepoint in a different medium. This one turned out
to be the largest, because everyone wants something.

## The infrastructure underneath

One further thing distinguishes this company from its predecessors, and it
becomes the decisive asset twenty years later.

Serving search at web scale on commodity hardware required a different kind of
computing, and Google built it: enormous numbers of inexpensive machines,
software that assumed individual machines would fail constantly, and distributed
systems for storing and processing data across all of them. The published papers
describing these systems in the early 2000s were read very widely and were
reimplemented in the open, which is where a substantial part of the modern data
infrastructure industry comes from.

The company then built its own data centres, sited for electricity and cooling,
and eventually designed its own chips.

The chapter marks this because Act IV's argument depends on it. A company that
begins by owning an index ends by owning the physical capacity to compute at
scale, and computing capacity turns out to be the chokepoint of the following
era. Vertical integration into the substrate — first the software, then the
buildings, then the silicon — is how a position in one layer becomes a position
in the layer beneath it.

## The appendix, again

Set the 1998 warning against the outcome.

They wrote that advertising funding creates a mixed incentive and that the bias
would be difficult for users to detect. Twenty-five years later, competition
authorities on two continents have concluded, in decisions running to hundreds
of pages, that the company gave preferential placement to its own services in
search results, and that it maintained its position in search through exclusive
default agreements with browser and device makers — including payments to Apple
of a scale that made Google the default on most of the world's phones.

Both of those findings describe the mechanism the appendix predicted.

The chapter does not need to editorialise and should not. The two documents sit
next to each other, written by the same people about the same system, twenty-
five years apart. The juxtaposition is the argument.

## The excluded

Three entries.

Users, whose behavioural data constitutes the asset and who receive the service
in exchange, on terms nobody negotiated and few have read.

Publishers, whose content is the raw material of the index and whose
relationship with their own audiences was intermediated by a company that
eventually competed with them for the same advertising revenue.

And advertisers, bidding in an auction whose rules and reserve prices they
cannot inspect — a fact that has been the subject of litigation on both sides of
the Atlantic.

The chokepoint is no longer physical, legal, or informational. It is
attentional, and it is the most profitable position anyone has ever found.
